hero.headline: Activists rally in Martin County to save deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce from shrimp trawling
hero.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. The reef, found hundreds of feet below the surface, is unique because it thrives in deep, dark waters unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive. The Oculina Bank is home to more than 2,000 marine species and exists nowhere else on Earth.

In January, the South Atlantic Marine Fishery Council voted to reopen more than 24 square nautical miles of the reef to shrimp trawling, an area larger than the island of Manhattan. Scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the rare reef, said he is very concerned about the ecosystem. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish," Gilmore said. Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, added that corals grow very slowly and have been there for a long time. "Corals are in trouble worldwide. We shouldn't be destroying anymore," Gilmore said.

Perry and Gilmore were two scientists who urged the public at the gathering to help save the reef. Perry said he was devastated by the council's decision. "Here's the same council that years ago, decades ago, approved protecting it, and that they now want to amend that protection and open it up to this destructive fishing effort," Perry said. The vote came despite tens of thousands of petition signatures opposing the move.

The proposal is now with NOAA, which will make the final decision. The agency is expected to release draft rules within the coming months, giving the public one more opportunity to weigh in before officials decide whether to move forward. Activists are urging residents to write letters to their congressman and those who might be able to influence the decisions. "All of our voices saying don't approve these amendments. We've got to protect these reefs," Perry said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie daughter charged with attempted murder after setting bedroom fire, attacking mother
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman faces attempted murder and arson charges after allegedly setting fire to a bedroom door while a 62-year-old woman was trapped inside Sunday night. Michelle Picard, 26, was arrested following the incident at a home in the 1500 block of Southeast Airoso Boulevard.

Port St. Lucie police responded to reports of a domestic disturbance and active house fire around 9:05 p.m. Officers found flames inside the residence and evacuated everyone safely. The investigation revealed the victim first noticed smoke coming from underneath her bedroom door and discovered Picard standing nearby when she opened it. When the victim attempted to retrieve a fire extinguisher, Picard allegedly physically attacked her and tried to prevent her from putting out the fire.

Police say Picard made threatening statements and attempted to push the victim toward the flames. The victim managed to escape to a bathroom, lock the door, and call 911. During the emergency call, Picard could be heard banging on the bathroom door in the background. Officers found Picard outside the residence and detained her. She resisted arrest, causing injuries to one officer's leg and requiring another officer to receive treatment for smoke inhalation. Both officers were treated at a local hospital and released.

Fire investigators determined the blaze was intentionally set. Picard faces charges of attempted murder, arson and resisting arrest without violence. Her total bond is $510,000. The victim was hospitalized for treatment of injuries sustained during the incident. The American Red Cross is assisting the victim with temporary housing and support services. Police emphasized this was an isolated domestic incident and there is no ongoing threat to the community.

cards.body:

Zamora, who previously had a romantic relationship with the victim, approached the woman despite an active injunction prohibiting any contact with her.

Police say Zamora, while armed with a handgun, grabbed the victim by her arms and attempted to force her into his vehicle against her will. The investigation revealed Zamora is a convicted felon who is prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition. Zamora faces five felony charges, including attempted kidnapping with a firearm, aggravated assault and battery of a person over 65. He is being held at St. Lucie County Jail on a $745,000 bond.

cards.headline: Florida Legislature approves DeSantis property tax cut plan for November ballot
cards.body:
The Florida Legislature has approved a property tax cut proposal backed by Governor Ron DeSantis, sending the measure to voters for consideration on the November ballot. The constitutional amendment passed during a special legislative session, marking a significant development in state tax policy that will affect property owners across Florida.

The proposal represents a major tax policy initiative that requires voter approval to take effect. As a constitutional amendment, the measure needs 60 percent support from Florida voters in the November election to become law. The legislative approval came after debate among state lawmakers about the potential impact on local government revenues and services. Jacksonville-area leaders have voiced concerns about the proposal, according to reports from the legislative session.

The property tax cut plan has drawn attention from business groups and local government officials statewide. The National Federation of Independent Business, which represents members across every industry in Florida, has been tracking the special session developments. Local leaders in multiple Florida regions have raised questions about how the tax cuts would affect funding for schools, public safety, and other services traditionally supported by property tax revenues.

Florida voters will make the final decision on the property tax amendment when they cast ballots in November. The measure represents one of the most significant fiscal policy questions facing the state this year. If approved by voters, the constitutional change would alter how property taxes are calculated and collected across all 67 Florida counties. The outcome will determine tax policy for homeowners, businesses, and local governments throughout the state for years to come. Lawmakers approved the measure during the special session convened specifically to address the tax proposal, demonstrating the priority state leadership has placed on the issue.

cards.headline: Martin County sheriff arrests three in retail theft ring that hit Stuart hardware stores, stole $500,000
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in Operation Hammer Time, a months-long investigation into a retail theft ring that targeted hardware stores across 13 counties. Major Ruben Romero said three suspects burglarized at least 40 stores from December 2025 to April 2026, including Sewell Hardware in Stuart, stealing roughly $500,000 worth of property and causing extensive damage.

Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, all from Miami-Dade County, are charged with racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, and burglary of occupied and unoccupied structures. Batista was arrested in February for vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, while Hernandez-Castro has an active warrant. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased.

The crews used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash store windows and complete thefts within minutes before police or alarms could respond. Stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, Jupiter and Broward County were targeted. The stolen goods were taken back to Miami-Dade County to be sold.

Romero said the thefts have real consequences for working people in the community. "There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are," he said. "People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools." Investigators believe burglaries occurred before December and are still looking for one additional suspect.

cards.body:
Five people were hospitalized Monday night after a multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 that also sparked a vehicle fire, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The collision occurred just before 10 p.m. on I-95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene, where they found one of the vehicles on fire. Crews quickly extinguished the flames.

Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to the hospital, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the crash. As of Tuesday morning, all lanes have reopened.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman left homeless after lightning strike destroys home, loses photos of late son
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera is displaced after a lightning strike caused a fire that destroyed her Fort Pierce home last month, leaving her without insurance and with almost nothing left.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce woman is displaced and calling for help after a lightning strike tore through her home, leaving her with broken windows, heavy damage, and almost nothing left. Last month, Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside. St. Lucie County District Firefighters rushed to put out the flames after the worker told her he believed her house was on fire. Rivera was told a lightning strike caused the fire.

Rivera lost clothes, furniture and irreplaceable personal belongings including photos of her late son. She is uninsured and is now staying at her nephew's home while she rebuilds. Rivera, who is also disabled, was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home. A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced.

Despite everything, Rivera said she is holding onto gratitude that she was not inside when the fire broke out. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood, FWC monitoring situation
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared video footage of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before running toward nearby homes.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The video, posted on the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Facebook page, shows the large black bear navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If it does not move from the area on its own, their bear biologists may set a trap to try and capture and relocate it. Port St. Lucie police stated that as Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions.

Wildlife officials emphasize specific protocols when encountering black bears in residential areas. If residents spot a bear, authorities recommend maintaining significant distance, never approaching the animal, and avoiding any attempts to feed it. Port St. Lucie police advise residents to keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties.

cards.headline: Former St. Lucie County school bus driver faces additional charge as second victim comes forward
cards.teaser: Edwin Garcia, 72, of Port St. Lucie, was arrested on a new battery charge May 28 when a second victim came forward in an ongoing investigation into allegations of inappropriate conduct with children.
cards.body:
A former St. Lucie County school bus driver is facing an additional charge after a second victim came forward in an ongoing investigation into allegations of inappropriate conduct with children. Edwin Garcia, 72, of Port St. Lucie, was arrested on a new battery charge May 28 when a second victim came forward with additional information for investigators. This comes after his initial arrest March 6 on two counts of lewd and lascivious molestation of a victim under 12 years of age.

The investigation began March 4 when a school resource deputy received a report that Garcia had allegedly asked a 9-year-old student to lift her dress while riding the school bus. During the preliminary investigation, deputies developed additional information suggesting Garcia may have made inappropriate comments to the child and possibly pinched her over her clothing in the pelvic area, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

The Sheriff's Office continues to investigate the allegations and is encouraging anyone who may have been a victim or has additional information to come forward. Anyone with information related to this case can contact Detective Corporal Hunter Limb at 772-462-7300 or email CrimeTips@stluciesheriff.gov.

hero.headline: Heiress donates land adjacent to Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve to block development
hero.body:
An heiress is purchasing and donating land near Hobe Sound to permanently protect it from development. The donated property sits adjacent to the Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve, one of the region's most important conservation areas.

The land acquisitions represent a significant conservation effort in northern Martin County, where development pressure has steadily increased. By purchasing the property and donating it for preservation, the heiress is ensuring that the acreage will remain undeveloped and contribute to the protection of the scrub ecosystem, which is home to endangered and threatened species.

The Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve encompasses coastal sand pine scrub habitat, which has become increasingly rare in Florida due to development. The preserve provides critical habitat for gopher tortoises, Florida scrub jays, and other native wildlife. Expanding the protected area through adjacent land donations strengthens the ecological corridor and reduces fragmentation.

The conservation effort comes as Martin County continues to grapple with balancing growth and environmental protection. Land preservation efforts like this one help maintain the natural character of communities like Hobe Sound while protecting the Indian River Lagoon watershed and coastal ecosystems that define the Treasure Coast.

hero.headline: Martin County sheriff arrests three in retail theft ring that hit Stuart hardware stores, stole $500,000
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in Operation Hammer Time, a months-long investigation into a retail theft ring that targeted hardware stores across 13 counties. Major Ruben Romero said three suspects burglarized at least 40 stores from December 2025 to April 2026, including Sewell Hardware in Stuart, stealing roughly $500,000 worth of property and causing extensive damage.

Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, all from Miami-Dade County, are charged with racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, and burglary of occupied and unoccupied structures. Batista was arrested in February for vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, while Hernandez-Castro has an active warrant. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased.

The crews used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash store windows and complete thefts within minutes before police or alarms could respond. Stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, Jupiter and Broward County were targeted. The stolen goods were taken back to Miami-Dade County to be sold.

Romero said the thefts have real consequences for working people in the community. "There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are," he said. "People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools." Investigators believe burglaries occurred before December and are still looking for one additional suspect.

cards.teaser: An heiress is purchasing land in Florida to prevent development and preserve natural areas from further urbanization.
cards.body:
An heiress is buying land in Florida to stop development and protect natural areas from being converted to residential or commercial use. The land purchases represent a private conservation effort to preserve open space in areas facing development pressure.

Florida has experienced rapid population growth and development over recent decades, putting pressure on remaining natural lands and wildlife habitat. Private conservation efforts supplement government land purchases and zoning regulations aimed at protecting environmentally sensitive areas.

The specific locations and extent of the land purchases were not detailed by officials. Private land conservation has become an increasingly important tool for protecting Florida's natural resources as development continues to spread into previously rural areas across the state.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman charged with attempted murder after setting fire to home with 62-year-old woman inside
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman is in custody facing attempted murder and arson charges after allegedly setting fire to a bedroom door while a 62-year-old woman was inside the room Sunday night. Michelle Picard, 26, was arrested following the incident on Southeast Airoso Boulevard in the 1500 block.

Port St. Lucie police responded to reports of a domestic disturbance and active house fire around 9:05 p.m. Sunday. Officers arriving at the scene found flames inside the residence and immediately worked to evacuate everyone. The investigation revealed that the victim first noticed smoke coming from underneath her bedroom door and discovered Picard standing nearby when she opened it. When the victim attempted to retrieve a fire extinguisher, Picard allegedly physically attacked her and tried to prevent her from putting out the fire. Police say Picard made threatening statements and attempted to push the victim toward the flames. The victim managed to escape to a bathroom, lock the door, and call 911. During the emergency call, Picard could be heard banging on the bathroom door in the background.

Officers found Picard outside the residence and detained her. She resisted arrest, causing injuries to one officer's leg and requiring another officer to receive treatment for smoke inhalation. Both officers were treated at a local hospital and released. The victim was also hospitalized for treatment of injuries sustained during the incident. Fire investigators determined the blaze was intentionally set.

Picard faces charges of attempted murder, arson and resisting arrest without violence. Her total bond is set at $510,000. The fire damaged the residence, and the American Red Cross is assisting the victim with temporary housing and support services. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Criminal Investigations Division, Crime Scene Investigators, St. Lucie County Fire District, and the State Fire Marshal's Office all responded to investigate. Police emphasized this was an isolated domestic incident and there is no ongoing threat to the community.

cards.headline: North Miami man arrested after attempting to kidnap woman at Port St. Lucie church
cards.teaser: Jose Tsu Zamora faces felony charges including attempted kidnapping with a firearm after allegedly trying to force a 74-year-old woman into his vehicle at First United Methodist Church Sunday morning.
cards.body:
A North Miami man was arrested Sunday evening after allegedly attempting to kidnap a 74-year-old woman in the parking lot of First United Methodist Church on Southwest Prima Vista Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. Jose Tsu Zamora, 64, was taken into custody by Port St. Lucie Police and U.S. Marshals at a residence in Hialeah.

The incident occurred around 10:49 a.m. Sunday morning. According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, Zamora approached the victim despite an active injunction prohibiting any contact with her. The two had previously been in a romantic relationship. Police say Zamora, while armed with a handgun, grabbed the victim by her arms and attempted to force her into his vehicle against her will. Several witnesses saw the incident and immediately intervened. Two Good Samaritans confronted Zamora and ordered him to release the victim. During the confrontation, Zamora displayed his firearm before retreating to his vehicle and fleeing the scene.

Church surveillance footage captured portions of the encounter and corroborated witness statements, showing Zamora pursuing the victim through the parking lot and physically restraining her. The investigation revealed Zamora is a convicted felon who is prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition. He faces five felony charges, including attempted kidnapping with a firearm, aggravated assault and battery of a person over 65. Zamora is being held at St. Lucie County Jail on a $745,000 bond.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage of a black bear swimming through the Town Park community Tuesday before running toward nearby homes, marking an unusual wildlife sighting along the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The video, posted on the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Facebook page, shows the large black bear navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If it doesn't move from the area on its own, their bear biologists may set a trap to try and capture and relocate it.

Port St. Lucie police explained the sighting as part of seasonal patterns. As Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. While seeing a bear may be surprising, it is not necessarily cause for alarm, police stated on Facebook. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions, making Tuesday's Port St. Lucie encounter particularly noteworthy for local residents.

Wildlife officials emphasize specific protocols when encountering black bears in residential areas. If residents spot a bear, authorities recommend maintaining significant distance, never approaching the animal, and avoiding any attempts to feed it. Port St. Lucie police advise residents to keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties. During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm and avoiding running. Instead, residents should slowly back away while keeping the bear visible, speak in calm, firm tones, and ensure the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman displaced after lightning strike destroys home, loses photos of late son
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera is calling for help after a lightning strike last month tore through her Fort Pierce home, leaving her with heavy damage and the loss of irreplaceable belongings including photos of her son who passed away three years ago.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce woman is displaced and calling for help after a lightning strike tore through her home, leaving her with broken windows, heavy damage, and almost nothing left. Last month, Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside. When I go back home, I see, the utility guy tells me, hey I think your house is on fire, Rivera said. St. Lucie County District Firefighters rushed to put out the flames. Rivera was told a lightning strike caused the fire.

Walking into her damaged home left her stunned. I was in shock, I'm thinking that's just a dream, but no, it's reality, Rivera said. Rivera lost clothes, furniture and irreplaceable personal belongings including photos of her late son. My son's pictures. My son passed away three years ago, Rivera said. The damage left Rivera displaced. She is uninsured and is now staying at her nephew's home while she rebuilds. I'm truly grateful for him, Rivera said. Because without him, I don't know where I would be.

Rivera, who is also disabled, was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home. It's a lot that I'm dealing with. It's very, very overwhelming, Rivera said. A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced. Despite everything, Rivera said she is holding onto one thing: gratitude that she was not inside when the fire broke out. It's a blessing that I was not home, Rivera said. And I was in a safe place instead of being at home to where something could've possibly happened to me. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild.

cards.headline: Former St. Lucie County school bus driver faces additional charge as second victim comes forward
cards.teaser: Edwin Garcia, 72, of Port St. Lucie, was arrested on a new battery charge May 28 after a second victim came forward with additional information for investigators.
cards.body:
A former St. Lucie County school bus driver is facing an additional charge after a second victim came forward in an ongoing investigation into allegations of inappropriate conduct with children. Edwin Garcia, 72, of Port St. Lucie, was arrested on a new battery charge May 28 when a second victim came forward with additional information for investigators. This comes after his initial arrest March 6 on two counts of lewd and lascivious molestation of a victim under 12 years of age.

The investigation began March 4 when a school resource deputy received a report that Garcia had allegedly asked a 9-year-old student to lift her dress while riding the school bus. During the preliminary investigation, deputies developed additional information suggesting Garcia may have made inappropriate comments to the child and possibly pinched her over her clothing in the pelvic area, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The case was then referred to the Criminal Investigations Division, leading to Garcia's initial arrest two days later on March 6.

The Sheriff's Office continues to investigate the allegations and is encouraging anyone who may have been a victim or has additional information to come forward. Anyone with information related to this case can contact Detective Corporal Hunter Limb at (772) 462-7300 or email CrimeTips@stluciesheriff.gov.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination
cards.teaser: A historic Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 has officially reopened as a new dining experience, bringing fresh energy to downtown Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
A historic Fort Pierce landmark is entering a new chapter. The Boston House, a downtown staple for more than a century, has officially reopened as a new dining experience, bringing fresh energy to a city working to redefine its future. Built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive, the home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served a variety of roles over the decades. Now, its newest owners are working to preserve its past while reimagining its purpose.

Fort Pierce is eclectic, artistic, deep, beautiful history, said co-owner Georgette Angelos. Behind its historic doors, the goal is simple: make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy. I want them to feel at home automatically, Angelos said. Originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway, who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the Boston House remains closely tied to the region's early development. It's keeping the authenticity so intact while also bringing a new breath of fresh air into the town that's so necessary right now, Angelos said.

During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details, including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past. General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown. Fort Pierce has had a reputation, and they really have done a great job bringing new life to the downtown area, Laird said. Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere. I think it's really important to hold onto the greatness we have in this area and really shine a spotlight on it, Laird said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Fire District honors fallen firefighter Connor Whitehead
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Fire District honored firefighter Connor Whitehead after his death.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District honored firefighter Connor Whitehead following his death. The fire district paid tribute to Whitehead, recognizing his service to the community and his fellow firefighters.

The ceremony brought together members of the fire district and the local community to remember Whitehead's dedication and sacrifice. Firefighters and officials gathered to honor his memory and the contributions he made during his time serving St. Lucie County residents.

The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to support Whitehead's family and colleagues during this time. The memorial service reflected the tight bonds within the firefighting community and the impact Whitehead had on those who worked alongside him.

hero.headline: Indian River Mall Demolition Underway in Vero Beach, Plans for Redevelopment Revealed
hero.body:
Demolition has begun at Indian River Mall in Vero Beach, with the former Macy's anchor store among the first structures coming down. The partial demolition marks a significant transformation for the shopping center that has served the community for decades.

The mall redevelopment represents a major change for Vero Beach retail and commercial landscape. Plans for the site's future have been released, showing what the reimagined property could look like once demolition and construction are complete. The transformation reflects broader trends affecting traditional shopping malls across Florida and the country.

Photos from the mall's heyday show the property during its peak years as a bustling retail destination for Indian River County shoppers. The images capture the mall when it served as a central gathering place and shopping hub for residents throughout the area.

The redevelopment project will reshape a key commercial corridor in Vero Beach. As demolition continues, the community waits to see how the transformed property will serve the area's changing retail and commercial needs in the years ahead.

cards.headline: World War II Veteran Bill Keegan Celebrates 102nd Birthday in Indian River County
cards.teaser: A World War II veteran marked his 102nd birthday with a motorcycle ride in Indian River County, celebrating more than a century of life.
cards.body:
Bill Keegan, a World War II veteran living in Indian River County, celebrated his 102nd birthday with a special motorcycle ride. The centenarian marked the milestone occasion in a memorable way that reflected his adventurous spirit.

Keegan's birthday celebration highlights the dwindling number of World War II veterans still living in the community. The men and women who served during that conflict are now in their late 90s and beyond, making each birthday an increasingly rare and noteworthy occasion.

The motorcycle ride gave Keegan a chance to enjoy the Florida weather and celebrate his longevity with family and supporters. His 102 years span more than a century of American history, from the 1920s through the present day, including his service during World War II and decades of life in Indian River County.

cards.headline: Indian River County Restaurant Inspections: One Perfect Score, One Failure
cards.teaser: Recent health inspections in Indian River County produced contrasting results, with one restaurant earning a perfect score while another failed its inspection.
cards.body:
Health inspectors visited restaurants across Indian River County, with results ranging from perfect to failing. One restaurant achieved a perfect score on its inspection, demonstrating full compliance with all food safety requirements and health standards.

Another restaurant in the county failed its health inspection. The failures indicate violations of health code requirements that could pose risks to diners. Failed inspections typically require immediate corrective action and follow-up visits from health inspectors.

Restaurant inspection scores are public records designed to help residents make informed decisions about where to dine. The inspections cover food handling practices, temperature control, cleanliness, pest control, and other factors that affect food safety. Restaurants must address violations and pass reinspection to continue operating.

cards.headline: Historical Marker Honors Florida Woman in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: A Florida woman's contributions are now commemorated with a historical marker in Vero Beach, recognizing her place in local history.
cards.body:
Vero Beach has added a new historical marker honoring a Florida woman whose contributions have earned recognition in the community. The marker serves as a permanent reminder of her role in local history and provides residents and visitors with information about her life and accomplishments.

Historical markers help preserve and share important stories from a community's past. They identify significant locations, commemorate notable residents, and educate the public about events and people who shaped the area. The markers become part of the historical landscape, offering educational value for generations to come.

The placement of the marker in Vero Beach adds to the collection of historical commemorations throughout Indian River County. These markers help residents and visitors understand the rich history of the area and the people who contributed to its development over the decades.

cards.headline: Indian River County Continues Review of Racquet Club Request
cards.teaser: Indian River County officials are continuing to review a request related to the Racquet Club, with the matter remaining under consideration.
cards.body:
Indian River County continues its review of a request involving the Racquet Club property. County officials are working through the details of the proposal as they evaluate the request and its implications for the area.

The ongoing review process indicates that county officials are taking time to carefully consider the request before making a decision. Local government reviews of property-related requests typically involve examining zoning requirements, community impact, and compliance with county regulations and comprehensive plans.

The Racquet Club matter remains active as county staff and officials work through the evaluation process. Residents interested in the outcome can follow the progress through county commission meetings and official updates as the review continues.

cards.headline: Space Jellyfish Phenomenon Explained as Rocket Launches Create Unique Contrails
cards.teaser: The unusual visual effect known as space jellyfish occurs during certain rocket launches, creating distinctive contrails visible from Florida's Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
The space jellyfish phenomenon creates a striking visual display during specific rocket launch conditions. The effect gets its name from the jellyfish-like appearance of rocket contrails that form under certain atmospheric conditions, often visible to viewers across Florida including the Treasure Coast.

The phenomenon occurs when rockets launch during twilight hours, with the sun below the horizon for ground observers but still illuminating the rocket at high altitude. As the rocket climbs and releases exhaust, the sunlight hits the expanding plume of gases and particles, creating a glowing, translucent effect that resembles a jellyfish floating in the sky.

Treasure Coast residents have opportunities to witness space jellyfish during launches from Cape Canaveral and Kennedy Space Center, located north of Indian River County. The effect requires specific timing and atmospheric conditions, making each sighting a somewhat rare and memorable event for those lucky enough to see it. Clear skies and launches during dawn or dusk provide the best chances for viewing the phenomenon.

cards.headline: Manatees Gather in Indian River Lagoon Near Cocoa
cards.teaser: Manatees congregated in the Indian River Lagoon near Cocoa for mating activity, with video capturing the gathering of the marine mammals.
cards.body:
Manatees gathered in the Indian River Lagoon near Cocoa for a mating event, with multiple animals coming together in the waters. Video footage captured the manatees as they engaged in mating behavior in the lagoon, providing a glimpse of the natural cycle of these protected marine mammals.

The Indian River Lagoon serves as critical habitat for manatees year-round, providing food sources, warm water refuges, and areas for mating and calving. Manatee mating gatherings typically involve multiple males pursuing a single female, creating groups that can be visible from shore or boats.

While this gathering occurred in the Cocoa area north of Indian River County, the lagoon system extends through the Treasure Coast and similar manatee activity occurs throughout the waterway. The lagoon remains one of the most important habitats for Florida's manatee population, and protecting water quality and seagrass beds in the system is vital for the species' long-term survival.
